distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical disease leaf for sinus node dysfunction causing inappropriate sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses or arrest, sinoatrial exit block, chronotropic incompetence, and tachy-brady atrial arrhythmia phenotypes.
distillation_scope.subtype_policy: Intrinsic degeneration, atrial remodeling, medication effect, autonomic or sleep-related suppression, metabolic-endocrine suppression, ischemic or inflammatory injury, and post-procedural states are represented as mechanisms, axes, risk factors, and treatment modifiers rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume rhythm strips, ECG or ambulatory-monitor evidence, symptom-rhythm correlation, heart-rate trajectory, pauses, chronotropic response, atrial tachyarrhythmias, syncope or presyncope, low-output physiology, reversible-cause context, pacing context, and thromboembolic risk when the evidence stage includes it. Later device follow-up, treatment response, and discharge diagnosis remain confirmatory unless a post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: The sinoatrial node generates impulses too slowly or unreliably for physiologic demand, producing inappropriate sinus bradycardia and low resting heart rate.
Sinus impulses fail to exit the node or atrial tissue, creating dropped atrial activation, sinoatrial block patterns, and episodic pauses.
Sinus impulse generation stops transiently, producing prolonged pauses, escape rhythm dependence, syncope, and bradycardic arrest hazard when escape activity is inadequate.
Sinus rate cannot rise appropriately during exertion, illness, or physiologic stress, producing exercise intolerance, fatigue, and exertional dyspnea despite acceptable resting rate.
Atrial remodeling produces paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, or atrial tachycardia alternating with sinus suppression and post-tachycardia pauses.
Slow rate, long pauses, or poor chronotropic reserve reduce cardiac output and cerebral perfusion, causing dizziness, presyncope, syncope, hypotension, shock, lactate rise, and organ injury hazard.
Age-related or idiopathic fibrosis of sinus-node tissue, perinodal atrium, and atrial conduction substrate makes dysfunction chronic, recurrent, and less reversible.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Reversible autonomic, drug, or metabolic sinus suppression
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Sinus-node function can be suppressed by rate-slowing drugs, high vagal tone, sleep apnea physiology, hypothyroidism, electrolyte disturbance, hypothermia, ischemia, inflammation, or other reversible stressors.
Residual ability of the sinus node to recover after reversible drivers are corrected, determined by fibrosis burden, atrial disease, ischemic or inflammatory injury, and chronicity.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Automaticity failure is the central hidden driver of the sinus-node dysfunction finding.
Slow sinus impulse generation appears clinically as bradycardia.
The bradycardia is sinus in origin when P-wave morphology and atrial activation remain sinus.
Reduced sinus automaticity lowers the observed heart rate.
Exit conduction failure is expressed as sinoatrial exit block on rhythm analysis.
Dropped sinus impulses create pauses in atrial and ventricular activation.
Transient cessation of sinus impulse formation is sinus arrest.
If escape activity is delayed, sinus arrest can appear as an asystolic pause.
Pause instability lengthens measured ventricular pause duration.
Escape rhythm may appear when sinus impulses fail or pause.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Escape rhythm may appear when sinus impulses fail or pause. Conditionality from original effect: increase_when_escape_available.

mechanism_edges.rationale: A weak sinus rate response is expressed as chronotropic incompetence.
Chronotropic incompetence lowers peak exertional heart-rate response relative to predicted need.
Insufficient rate rise during activity limits cardiac output reserve.
Poor rate response can manifest as chronic fatigue or low exertional capacity.
Low exertional cardiac output can be perceived as exertional dyspnea.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Low exertional cardiac output can be perceived as exertional dyspnea. Conditionality from original effect: increase_with_exertion.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Alternation between atrial tachyarrhythmia and sinus suppression defines the tachy-brady phenotype.
Atrial remodeling frequently expresses as paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
Atrial remodeling can also express as atrial flutter.
Some patients express atrial tachycardia or other supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.
Sinus-node recovery can be delayed after termination of atrial tachyarrhythmia.
Intermittent atrial tachyarrhythmia can cause palpitations.
Atrial fibrillation or flutter in the tachy-brady phenotype can raise thromboembolic stroke hazard.
Cerebral hypoperfusion can cause dizziness.
Near-syncope reflects transient cerebral hypoperfusion.
More severe or abrupt cerebral hypoperfusion can cause syncope.
Syncope from bradycardia can lead to falls.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Syncope from bradycardia can lead to falls. Conditionality from original effect: increase_when_syncope_occurs.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Low rate and pauses reduce cardiac output enough to lower MAP in vulnerable patients.
Bradycardic low output can lower systolic pressure when compensation is insufficient.
Systemic arterial pressure can fall during sustained bradycardia or long pauses.
Severe hypoperfusion can raise lactate.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Severe hypoperfusion can raise lactate. Conditionality from original effect: increase_if_shock.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Uncorrected bradycardic low output raises cardiogenic shock hazard.
Prolonged pauses and failed escape activity raise bradycardic arrest hazard.
Fibrosis makes the disease context chronic or degenerative.
Fixed fibrotic substrate lowers the probability of native sinus-node recovery.
Persistent fibrotic sinus-node dysfunction strengthens durable pacing context.
Rate-slowing medication exposure can be a reversible suppressor of sinus-node function.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Rate-slowing medication exposure can be a reversible suppressor of sinus-node function. Conditionality from original effect: increase_context_dependent.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Sleep-related autonomic surges or high vagal tone can suppress sinus activity.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Sleep-related autonomic surges or high vagal tone can suppress sinus activity. Conditionality from original effect: increase_context_dependent.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Hypothyroid context can be reflected by elevated TSH when present.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Hypothyroid context can be reflected by elevated TSH when present. Conditionality from original effect: increase_if_hypothyroid_context.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Low free thyroxine supports endocrine suppression when hypothyroidism is the driver.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Low free thyroxine supports endocrine suppression when hypothyroidism is the driver. Conditionality from original effect: decrease_if_hypothyroid_context.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Electrolyte disturbance can suppress nodal automaticity or conduction.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Electrolyte disturbance can suppress nodal automaticity or conduction. Conditionality from original effect: abnormal_if_electrolyte_context.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Reversible suppression increases recovery probability after cause correction.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Reversible suppression increases recovery probability after cause correction. Conditionality from original effect: increase_if_reversible_driver.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Recovery capacity is observed as the probability of sinus-node recovery without durable pacing dependence.
Stable recovery reduces need for temporary pacing support.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Stable recovery reduces need for temporary pacing support. Conditionality from original effect: decrease_when_recovery_high_and_stable.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Mortality hazard rises when bradycardic hypoperfusion becomes shock, recurrent syncope injury, or refractory low-output physiology.
Long pauses with inadequate escape activity can acutely increase death hazard.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Long pauses with inadequate escape activity can acutely increase death hazard. Conditionality from original effect: increase_if_prolonged_pause_or_escape_failure.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Atrial tachyarrhythmia contributes to mortality mainly through thromboembolism, heart failure stress, or unstable rhythm transitions.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Atrial tachyarrhythmia contributes to mortality mainly through thromboembolism, heart failure stress, or unstable rhythm transitions. Conditionality from original effect: increase_if_stroke_or_unstable_arrhythmia.
Bradycardic low-output episodes can transiently reduce cerebral or retinal perfusion and cause visual dimming.
Sinus pause/arrest instability increases severity of bradycardia episodes.
Low-output bradycardia may coexist with or worsen congestive physiology.
Hemodynamic stress and heart failure physiology can elevate BNP in symptomatic bradyarrhythmia.
Structural atrial/heart disease context can accompany degenerative sinus-node disease.
Long sinus pauses can be followed by slow junctional or ventricular escape rhythm.

axes.shape_free_text: Any clinically meaningful rhythm abnormality on ECG, rhythm strip, telemetry, or ambulatory monitoring.
Evidence that the sinus node or sinoatrial conduction is the origin of bradycardia, pauses, arrest, or chronotropic failure.
axes.clinical_interpretation: Sick sinus syndrome requires positive sinus-node dysfunction evidence such as inappropriate sinus bradycardia, pauses/arrest, SA exit block, tachy-brady pattern, or chronotropic incompetence. Generic tachycardia or shock-related heart-rate change must not satisfy this source geometry.

axes.shape_free_text: Heart rate lower than physiologic need for age, activity, and clinical context.
Bradycardia with sinus P-wave morphology and sinus activation pattern.
axes.clinical_interpretation: Sinus bradycardia supports sinus-node disease when paired with pauses or tachy-brady symptoms.

axes.shape_free_text: Observed heart rate; sick sinus syndrome often lowers resting rate or creates alternating low and high-rate episodes.
Lowest heart rate captured on ECG, telemetry, ambulatory monitor, or wearable rhythm evidence.
Intermittent absence of expected sinus impulses producing a pause.
axes.clinical_interpretation: Documented sinus pauses are core sick-sinus evidence.

axes.shape_free_text: Pause pattern consistent with transient cessation of sinus impulse formation.
Rhythm pattern indicating intermittent failure of sinus impulses to conduct from the sinus node to atrial tissue.
Long pause with absent effective ventricular activation before sinus recovery or escape rhythm.
axes.clinical_interpretation: Long pauses caused by sinus arrest or sinus pause are a direct manifestation of sick sinus syndrome.

axes.shape_free_text: Measured duration of ventricular pause on rhythm evidence.
axes.clinical_interpretation: Sick sinus syndrome can produce prolonged symptomatic pauses; very long pauses should remain compatible.

axes.shape_free_text: Junctional or ventricular escape activity after sinus slowing or pause.
Failure to increase sinus rate appropriately with exercise, stress, or physiologic demand.
Percent of age- and context-predicted heart-rate response achieved during exertion or chronotropic testing.
Reduced ability to exert due to inadequate rate or cardiac output response.
Alternation of atrial tachyarrhythmia with sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, or post-tachycardia suppression.
Atrial fibrillation documented during the tachy-brady phenotype.
Atrial flutter documented during the tachy-brady phenotype.
Intermittent atrial tachycardia or supraventricular tachyarrhythmia that may alternate with bradycardia.
Sinus pause immediately after spontaneous or treated termination of atrial tachyarrhythmia.
Symptoms occur at the same time as sinus bradycardia, pause, arrest, or tachy-brady transition on rhythm evidence.
Transient loss of consciousness from suspected or documented cerebral hypoperfusion.
Near-fainting, lightheadedness, or impending syncope without complete loss of consciousness.
Dizziness or lightheadedness that may reflect intermittent cerebral hypoperfusion.
Fatigue or low energy from chronic low rate or chronotropic incompetence.
Dyspnea, especially exertional dyspnea, from inadequate cardiac output response or coexisting cardiac disease.
Awareness of intermittent atrial tachyarrhythmia, rhythm transition, or compensatory beats.
Fall temporally associated with suspected or documented bradycardic syncope.
Systolic arterial pressure; may fall during severe bradycardia or prolonged pauses.
Diastolic arterial pressure during bradycardic or low-output episodes.
Mean arterial pressure, lowered when bradycardic low-output physiology overwhelms compensation.
Clinically relevant low blood pressure during bradycardia, pause, or low-output state.
Lactate elevation when severe bradycardic hypoperfusion produces systemic shock physiology.
Context that intrinsic sinus-node or atrial fibrosis is likely, based on age, chronicity, recurrence, and absence of a clearly reversible driver.
Exposure to medications that can slow sinus-node automaticity or exacerbate pauses.

axes.display_name: Sleep apnea or high vagal tone context presence
axes.shape_free_text: Context for nocturnal, sleep-related, reflex, or vagally mediated sinus slowing or pauses.
TSH as part of endocrine context when hypothyroidism may contribute to bradycardia.
Free T4 as part of endocrine context when hypothyroidism may contribute to sinus-node suppression.
Potassium abnormality that may worsen bradycardia, nodal automaticity, or conduction.

axes.display_name: Metabolic or endocrine reversible context presence
axes.shape_free_text: Potentially reversible metabolic, endocrine, electrolyte, or hypothermia context contributing to sinus-node suppression.

axes.display_name: Ischemic or inflammatory sinus-node injury context presence
axes.shape_free_text: Context that sinus-node dysfunction is driven by ischemia, myocarditis, infiltrative disease, inflammatory disease, or periatrial injury.

axes.display_name: Post cardiac surgery or ablation context presence
axes.shape_free_text: Recent cardiac surgery, atrial surgery, maze procedure, ablation, or structural intervention context that can injure sinus-node tissue or atrial conduction.
Estimated probability that sinus-node function recovers after reversible drivers are removed or acute injury improves.
Context that acute electrical rate support is needed because bradycardia or pauses threaten perfusion before recovery or durable device decision.
Context that durable pacing support is needed due to persistent or recurrent symptomatic sinus-node dysfunction, pauses, or chronotropic incompetence.
Context that pacing needs dynamic rate response because chronotropic incompetence is a major driver of symptoms.
Context that atrial fibrillation or flutter carries enough thromboembolic risk to modify stroke-prevention treatment effect.
Hazard of traumatic injury from recurrent bradycardic syncope or falls.
Hazard of shock from sustained bradycardic low output or prolonged pauses.
Hazard of pulseless arrest from extreme bradycardia, prolonged pause, or escape failure.
Hazard of unstable rhythm events in the setting of atrial arrhythmia transitions, pauses, ischemia, electrolyte disturbance, or device complications.
Hazard of embolic stroke from atrial fibrillation or flutter in the tachy-brady phenotype.
Hazard of major bleeding when stroke-prevention anticoagulation or procedural context is active.
Hazard of lead, pocket, infection, perforation, thrombosis, capture, or pacing-induced complication after pacing intervention.

axes.display_name: Mortality hazard in sick sinus syndrome
axes.shape_free_text: Disease-specific lifespan outcome hazard emerging from prolonged pauses, bradycardic arrest, shock, traumatic syncope, thromboembolic stroke, malignant arrhythmia context, comorbidity, and treatment complications.

axes.clinical_interpretation: Transient visual dimming or amaurosis can accompany bradycardic cerebral hypoperfusion in sick sinus syndrome; persistent focal visual deficit should be evaluated as a neurologic disorder.

axes.shape_free_text: Bradycardic low-output or tachy-brady heart failure context can produce pulmonary congestion.
Severity of sinus bradycardia or pauses in sick sinus syndrome.
BNP may rise when bradycardia/tachy-brady syndrome contributes to heart failure physiology.
Cardiomegaly context can coexist with sick sinus syndrome and low-output heart failure.
Escape rhythm rate during sinus arrest or severe sinus bradycardia.
Somnolence is not intrinsic to sinus-node disease, but may coexist when high intracranial pressure or mass effect is the reversible autonomic trigger.
Altered mental status attributable to high-ICP or mass-effect context rather than primary sinus-node tissue disease.
Nausea may accompany intracranial pressure elevation in secondary sinus-pause presentations.
Nausea or vomiting burden from intracranial pressure context in secondary sinus-pause presentations.
Focal weakness may coexist when the trigger for sinus pauses is intracranial mass effect or recent neurosurgical disease.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Sinus-node dysfunction is usually expressed by inappropriate bradycardia when pauses or tachy episodes are not dominating.
Observed bradycardia directly corresponds to low measured heart rate.
A rhythm strip pause is quantified by ventricular pause duration.
Longer pauses are more likely to cause cerebral hypoperfusion and syncope.
Termination of atrial tachyarrhythmia can be followed by a pause long enough to cause syncope.
Failure to raise heart rate during exertion limits cardiac output reserve.
Atrial fibrillation or flutter increases embolic stroke hazard in susceptible patients.
Below the compensation range, bradycardia lowers cardiac output and MAP.
Persistent hypotension during bradycardia increases shock hazard.
Recurrent syncope can lead to falls and traumatic injury.
Bradycardic arrest is a direct contributor to death hazard.
Shock from bradycardic low output increases death hazard until rate support or cause correction restores perfusion.
Stroke hazard contributes to long-horizon mortality risk in tachy-brady phenotypes.
Major bleeding is a treatment-context event hazard that can reduce survival benefit when bleeding risk is high.
Serious pacing-device complications can offset benefit in vulnerable patients.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: If native recovery probability is high, immediate durable device effect depends on persistence and recurrence.
Rate-response programming matters more when chronotropic incompetence drives symptoms.

treatments.context_specific_role: Durable electrical rate support for persistent or recurrent symptomatic sinus-node dysfunction, pauses, and chronotropic incompetence.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Atrial tachyarrhythmia can complicate rate-response settings.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjusts device behavior when symptoms persist because rate response does not match physiologic demand.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Transcutaneous pacing is a short bridge and can be poorly tolerated.

treatments.context_specific_role: Immediate noninvasive bridge for unstable bradycardia or prolonged pauses while more durable support or cause correction is arranged.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Temporary pacing bridges a persistent low-recovery substrate to durable support.

treatments.context_specific_role: Invasive temporary bridge when unstable bradycardia or pause risk persists beyond immediate noninvasive support.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Intrinsic sinus-node fibrosis may not respond strongly to vagolytic therapy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Short-acting chronotropic push when vagal tone or nodal suppression contributes and while electrical support remains available if response is inadequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Catecholamine chronotropy can provoke atrial or ventricular arrhythmias.

treatments.context_specific_role: Pharmacologic bridge for unstable bradycardic low-output physiology when pacing is delayed, unavailable, or being prepared.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Stopping suppressing drugs may not fully reverse fixed sinus-node fibrosis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Removes an external suppressive vector when the medication timeline plausibly explains bradycardia or pauses.

treatments.display_name: Correct metabolic, endocrine, or electrolyte driver

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Metabolic correction may be slower than the immediate perfusion threat.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reshapes reversible endocrine, electrolyte, metabolic, or temperature-related suppression while pacing or chronotropic support handles acute instability.

treatments.display_name: Sleep apnea or autonomic trigger management

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Intrinsic fibrosis can remain even after nocturnal or vagal triggers improve.

treatments.context_specific_role: Modulates recurrent nocturnal or vagal suppression when rhythm evidence and context support that driver.

treatments.display_name: Atrial tachyarrhythmia control with brady-support context

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rate- or rhythm-controlling therapy can worsen bradycardia unless rate support context is handled.
Durable rate support can reduce the bradycardic penalty of tachyarrhythmia control.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces atrial tachyarrhythmia burden in tachy-brady phenotype while explicitly accounting for bradycardia and pacing context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Recurrent syncope and falls increase bleeding consequence if anticoagulated.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces thromboembolic hazard when atrial fibrillation or flutter is part of the sick sinus syndrome state.

risk_factors.display_name: Advanced age or degenerative atrial fibrosis

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Degenerative fibrosis increases chronic sinus-node dysfunction context.
Fixed substrate lowers native recovery probability.
Durable support context strengthens when dysfunction is chronic and recurrent.

treatment_effect_modulation.permanent_pacemaker_implantation: durable rate-support effect strengthens when recovery probability is low

risk_factors.display_name: Preexisting atrial fibrillation or atrial cardiomyopathy

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Atrial cardiomyopathy makes tachy-brady expression more likely.
Atrial arrhythmia burden increases embolic risk.

treatment_effect_modulation.anticoagulation_for_atrial_tachyarrhythm: stroke-prevention effect depends more on embolic-risk context

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Medication exposure becomes a visible reversible driver.
Stopping the drug can permit recovery when intrinsic fibrosis is limited.

treatment_effect_modulation.withdraw_sinus_node_suppressing_agents: effect strengthens when exposure timing matches bradycardia or pauses

risk_factors.display_name: Sleep apnea or high vagal tone

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Nocturnal or vagal context becomes more likely.
Autonomic surges can produce episodic pauses.

treatment_effect_modulation.permanent_pacemaker_implantation: benefit depends on persistence after reversible autonomic component is addressed

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Metabolic or endocrine abnormality becomes part of the disease state.
Correctable causes can improve recovery probability.

treatment_effect_modulation.temporary_pacing_need_context_presence: bridge context remains if instability precedes correction

risk_factors.display_name: Ischemic, inflammatory, or infiltrative cardiac disease

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Sinus-node or atrial injury context becomes more likely.
Coexisting myocardial disease increases unstable arrhythmia risk.

treatment_effect_modulation.chronotropic_vasoactive_infusion: ischemia or arrhythmia toxicity margin narrows
treatment_effect_modulation.permanent_pacemaker_implantation: device strategy may need ventricular function and arrhythmia context

risk_factors.display_name: Post cardiac surgery, ablation, or structural intervention

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Procedural atrial or sinus-node injury context becomes more likely.
Post-procedural dysfunction may recover or persist depending on substrate.

treatment_effect_modulation.permanent_pacemaker_implantation: durable support context strengthens if dysfunction persists

risk_factors.display_name: Low cardiac reserve or heart failure

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Limited stroke-volume reserve makes bradycardia less tolerated.
Comorbidity raises death hazard under the same rhythm burden.

treatment_effect_modulation.permanent_pacemaker_implantation: pacing configuration and ventricular synchrony context become more important
treatment_effect_modulation.chronotropic_vasoactive_infusion: perfusion benefit and arrhythmia or ischemia risk both increase

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Baseline embolic susceptibility increases stroke hazard from atrial tachyarrhythmia.
Thromboembolic-risk context strengthens stroke-prevention treatment relevance.

treatment_effect_modulation.anticoagulation_for_atrial_tachyarrhythm: stroke hazard reduction has larger outcome effect

risk_factors.display_name: High bleeding or recurrent fall risk context

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Falls increase injury hazard when syncope recurs.
Frailty, bleeding risk, or anticoagulation can increase procedural complication impact.

treatment_effect_modulation.permanent_pacemaker_implantation: procedural complication hazard weighs more in forward simulation

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Raised intracranial pressure can provoke high-vagal-tone sinus pauses.
Severe reflex sinus suppression can produce symptomatic pauses.
ICP-related autonomic pauses may be several seconds long.
Long pauses triggered by high ICP can cause syncope.
Somnolence belongs to the intracranial mass-effect context.
Mass effect can produce altered mental status alongside sinus pauses.
Raised ICP can cause nausea at presentation.
Raised ICP can produce nausea or vomiting symptoms.
Focal weakness can be explained by the neurologic mass-effect context.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Structural cardiomyopathy context can support sinus node dysfunction and pauses.
Stroke context does not define sick sinus syndrome but supports the clinical relevance of embolic bradyarrhythmia detection.

supportive_care.care_name: Continuous telemetry and rhythm strip review
supportive_care.rationale: Track sinus bradycardia, pauses, escape rhythm, atrial tachyarrhythmia transitions, capture, and symptom-rhythm correlation during acute risk assessment.
Capture intermittent sinus pauses, tachy-brady transitions, chronotropic response, atrial arrhythmia burden, and competing conduction abnormalities.
Maintain pads, venous access, capture monitoring, sedation or analgesia planning, and escalation route when bradycardia threatens perfusion.

supportive_care.care_name: Reversible cause medication and laboratory review
supportive_care.rationale: Review rate-slowing drugs, renal clearance, thyroid function, potassium and other electrolytes, hypothermia, ischemic or inflammatory context, and sleep-related triggers without converting them into diagnosis labels.

supportive_care.care_name: Syncope, fall, and activity risk precautions
supportive_care.rationale: Reduce traumatic harm while pauses, presyncope, or syncope remain active and before rate support or reversible-cause correction stabilizes the state.
Monitor sensing, thresholds, capture, lead position, pocket complications, infection, and pacing burden after temporary or permanent pacing.
Track atrial fibrillation or flutter burden, stroke hazard context, bleeding tradeoff, and interactions between rhythm control and bradycardia support.

quality_notes: Disease-only staging distillation; no real-case search or case structuring was performed.
The disease-specific medical input is limited to Disease: Sick sinus syndrome (id: D-SICK-SINUS-SYNDROME).
There is exactly one derived_hazard axis: mortality_hazard_in_D-SICK-SINUS-SYNDROME.
Treatment entries avoid rank labels; therapy ranking is left to forward simulation over rhythm burden, perfusion, reversibility, pacing context, thromboembolic hazard, and treatment complications.
2026-05-31 required-context repair: added sinus-node dysfunction gate so shock tachycardia cases cannot combine with sick sinus syndrome without ECG brady/pause/chronotropic evidence.
